Current: Lloyd's writes US business mainly as a surplus lines insurer and reinsurer; it's admitted only in Illinois, Kentucky and the US Virgin Islands.
Proposed: Lloyd's writes US business as a surplus lines (non-admitted) insurer in all states and as a reinsurer. It gave up its admitted licenses in Illinois, Kentucky and the US Virgin Islands, stopping admitted renewals from July 1, 2021.
Reason: Lloyd's announced in 2020 that it would relinquish its admitted licenses in IL, KY and USVI; the note describes the pre-2021 position.

Current: Florida restricted AOB for property claims in 2019 and 2022 after abuse; health providers routinely take AOB.
Proposed: Florida restricted AOBs for property claims in 2019, then banned them for residential and commercial property policies issued on or after January 1, 2023 (SB 2-A, 2022), and for auto glass claims under policies issued or renewed from July 1, 2023. Health providers routinely take AOBs.
Reason: 'Restricted' understates the 2022 change: SB 2-A prohibits AOBs under property policies issued on or after 1/1/2023; a 2023 law also voids auto-glass AOBs.

Proposed: ACA Marketplace open enrollment dates are set by federal rule and have been in flux: a 2025 CMS rule would have shortened the window (HealthCare.gov Nov 1-Dec 15) from 2027, but a federal court vacated that provision in June 2026 and the case is on appeal. Check HealthCare.gov or your state exchange for current dates. Employer plans set their own open enrollment.
Reason: The example (Nov 1-Jan 15) is currently right for 2027 coverage on HealthCare.gov, but only because the shortened window was vacated; the government has appealed (argument Oct 30, 2026), so the date may change. Several state exchanges also use different end dates.

Current: Licensed and fee-capped by state; some states cap fees after catastrophes.
Proposed: Licensed in most states. Only some states cap public adjuster fees (often at 10-20% of the claim payment), and several set lower caps after declared catastrophes, e.g., Florida's 10% cap on claims in the first year after a hurricane emergency.
Reason: 'Fee-capped by state' implies all states cap fees; roughly a third of licensing states have a statutory cap.

Proposed: Social Engineering Coverage; Fraudulent Instruction; Impersonation Fraud
Reason: Funds transfer fraud is a separate crime/cyber coverage for transfers made by a bank without the insured's knowledge; social engineering covers transfers an employee was tricked into making. Courts have denied social-engineering losses under funds transfer and computer fraud insuring agreements, so treating them as synonyms misleads.

Current: Most states limit backdating to 6 months.
Proposed: Backdating is commonly limited to 6 months, by state law in some states and by insurer practice elsewhere.
Reason: No source supports 'most states'; available sources say some states set a 6-month maximum and insurers apply their own limits.

Current: States set minimum notice periods (often 30–60 days) and sometimes restrict reasons.
Proposed: States set minimum notice periods (often 30-60 days, but longer for some lines, e.g., Florida requires 120 days for residential property) and sometimes restrict reasons.
Reason: The 30-60 day range misses important longer periods such as Florida's 120-day residential property rule.

Current: Not enforced in some states, such as California and Washington.
Proposed: Not enforced in a few states: California and North Dakota by statute, Washington and West Virginia by case law.
Reason: Correct but incomplete; four jurisdictions are commonly cited.

Current: Most states have TNC insurance laws.
Proposed: Nearly all states and D.C. have TNC insurance laws, typically requiring $1 million of TNC-provided liability once a ride is accepted.
Reason: Understated: TNC insurance laws exist in essentially every state.

Current: Several states have 'valued policy laws' requiring full face payment for total fire losses on buildings.
Proposed: About 17 states have 'valued policy laws' requiring full face payment for certain total losses to buildings; some apply only to fire or only to residential property.
Reason: More precise count available; scope varies by state.

Current: Some states (e.g., Florida, Kentucky, South Carolina) require zero-deductible windshield coverage.
Proposed: Florida, Kentucky and South Carolina require zero-deductible windshield coverage for drivers who carry comprehensive; several other states (e.g., Arizona, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New York) require insurers to offer a glass option.
Reason: Clarifies that the mandate applies only when comprehensive is carried.

Current: Adjusters must be licensed in most states.
Proposed: Most states license independent adjusters (about 35); licensing of insurer-employed staff adjusters varies by state.
Reason: 'Adjusters must be licensed in most states' is broadly right for independent adjusters but not for all staff adjusters.

Current: Most forms must be filed with and approved by state regulators.
Proposed: Most personal lines forms must be filed with and approved by state regulators; filing rules for commercial forms vary, and some large commercial risks are exempt.
Reason: 'Filed with and approved' overstates approval for commercial lines, where file-and-use and exemptions are common.
